language.howToChooseYourGradeContent:
It’s very important children start at the right level, have fun in learning and work at their own pace. Please help the children selecting the level that is not too easy, but also not too difficult for them. There are two ways to do this.

  • You can either check the learning goals yourself to determine the correct level for your child(ren).
  • Or you can let the child take several lessons to determine his or her level. For example, if your child has the age of 6, please let him or her take one lesson in grade K, one lesson in grade 1, and one lesson in grade 2 to determine at which level he or she is.

Antarctica is almost completely covered with ice. This continent is the coldest region on earth, the lowest temperature ever recorded was -91°C!

I am working here as a meteorologist, which means I study different weather patterns and the global climate. This is my friend Josh. The global climate affect Josh's  life here at Antarctica since global warming causes the snow and ice to melt. To understand more about this, I will teach you today about different weather types such as…

let's start!

Hi there! My name is Jane. Welcome to Antarctica! This is my home for 6 months! As you can see on the map, Antarctica is located very much south on the globe; therefore those are know as the South Pole.
Antarctica is almost completely covered with ice. This continent is the coldest region on earth, the lowest temperature ever recorded was -91°C!

I am working here as a meteorologist, which means I study different weather patterns and the global climate. This is my friend Josh. The global climate affect Josh's  life here at Antarctica since global warming causes the snow and ice to melt. To understand more about this, I will teach you today about different weather types such as…

…precipitation, cold and warm front, storms and hurricanes! So come on,
let's start!

There are different kinds of precipitation. With precipitation, we mean all types of liquid or solid water that falls from the atmosphere and reaches the surface of the Earth. Rain is by far the most common type of precipitation in our atmosphere.

Rain arises from water evaporation and that goes like this: When the sun shines on the water, the water heats up, this makes the water evaporate bit by bit. It rises up and high in the air it
forms a cloud.

If the water in the cloud gets too heavy, the water will fall down back to the earth, and this can be rain or
other precipitation.
Another type of precipitation is snow. Snow is formed when the temperatures are low. If it is cold, the evaporated water from the Earth turns into ice crystals in the air.
When these tiny ice crystals collide this stick together in clouds to become snowflakes. If enough ice crystals stick together, they'll become heavy enough to fall to the ground.
Precipitation falls as snow when the air temperature is below 2 °C.

The third type of precipitation is sleet. Sleet refers to a mixture of snow and rain as well as raindrops that freeze on their way down. Unlike snow, the raindrops pass through a liquid form before freezing. The result is that they are not light and fluffy. And watch out on the road if there is sleet, it makes it very slippery!
Another type of precipitation is hail. Hail is a complex combination between moisture and wind. Deep within clouds ice crystals form and begin to fall towards the Earth's surface.

As this happens, wind gusts pick up the ice crystals, pushing them back up high into the clouds. As they begin to fall down again, they continue growing in size. This continues until the little ice blocks are too heavy for the wind to carry. Let's take a look at the following questions. Can you answer them?

Wow! Well done!
You've now learned about the different types of precipitation. However, sometimes precipitation can form a combination with lots of wind to form a storm.
Huge storms take the form of hurricanes, typhoons or cyclones. They are all the same, but have different names in different places.
We use "Hurricane" in the Atlantic and Northeast Pacific, we say "Typhoon" if it is in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, and "Cyclones" if they are in the South Pacific and Indian Ocean.

The areas in which these huge storms occur are moist and warm. They start to form warm ocean water of 27 degrees Celsius or warmer. The warm moist air from the water mixes with the cold falling air form the sky.
A breeze makes them turn around, and the wind forces become stronger and stronger. Finally, the forces in the air start spinning and start to produce violent winds.
We call the center of the storm the "eye". In the eye, the winds are light and the weather is fair.
However, the rest of the hurricane can increase in strength and size and cause incredible waves, torrential rains, floods and damage to buildings, trees and cars.
If normal storms gets rougher and stronger, we start to call them tropical storms.
If this tropical storm gains strength and has winds spiraling inward and upward at speeds of 119 km per hour or more,
it becomes a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone. There are five strength categories of hurricanes, depending on the wind speed.
The highest category is 5 and that's above 249 kilometers per hour!!
Well, let's see what you know of these huge storms! Can you tell me which of these statements are true or false?

Thanks! Well done!

The story about precipitation gets a little bit more complicated. Because where or when precipitation will drop, does not only have to do with the moisture in the air, but also with what we call "warm" and "cold" fronts.
A front is the place where two air masses of different temperatures meet. Warm front is the zone where warm air mass is replacing a cold air mass. Warm air is lighter than cold air.

Therefore, the warm air gradually rises on top of the cold air, until it forms clouds high up in the sky. Then the moisture in the air cools down, and
forms precipitation.

This shows a cold front. We speak about a cold front if colder air is replacing warmer air. The cold air clashes with the warm air, and the warm air, which is lighter, will again rise above the cold air.

Because of the clash, the angle of the front becomes steeper and the warm air will rise rapidly. The fast climbing warm air then cools down and forms clouds very high up in the sky. These high clouds can cause heavy rain
or even storm.

You may have seen weather forecasts on television. When the weather man does his story, he uses a weather map, like this!

These maps show the weather forecast for the near future. Do you see the blue lines with the triangles? Those are cold fronts. The red lines with the bumps are the warm fronts. The arrows and the bumps point in the direction of the wind.
Because we know the speed of the wind, where the cold and warm fronts are located and in what direction they are going, we can predict the weather in different places.
Weather maps have big H's and L's on them. "H" stands for high pressure area. "L" stands for low pressure area. High pressure usually means nice weather, clear skies and no precipitation.
So, with the "H" you can think of "Happy" weather! The "L" stands for low pressure. Low pressure usually means bad weather. So, you could say "L" means "lousy" weather.
